title: Jack Purvis and Fred Waring's moustache
summary: Barnet recalls Purvis's wives and eccentricities, and how he was fired from Waring's Pennsylvanians over a moustache and shaved head, prompting the move south.

story.theme_name: Band pranks, jokes and gigs gone wrong
story.community_name: Pranks, practical jokes and band humor

blocks.x: I don't know what for. He had, oh, like seven or eight wives with no divorces, and he used to steal the Western Union boys' bicycles, and he was a thoroughly crazy man, but very talented. Well, I'll give you an example. When we left to go from New York down to Shreveport, Jack was playing first trumpet with Waring's Pennsylvanians, which of course was a very collegiate outfit, and he had been added to the band because Waring was playing at the Roxy Theater, and they had expanded the orchestra to -- you see the scene, in the pit, they were playing the Overture of 1812, which starts out with the trumpet. And now the little pin spot picks Waring up, he comes out of the wings, walks around and goes tip tip, and gives the down beat, and the pin spot comes on the trumpet player, which is Purvis. Now, Jack had a pride and joy of his, which was a little waxed moustache, which he kept cut, you know, and everything. And Waring, it upset him, Waring. Waring said, "Look, Jack," he said, "this is a

college band, Waring's Pennsylvanians. You look like a French count or something. Now please take that off." So Jack cut it off, but he also cut every hair on his head off, he shaved his head. So the next show, here comes Waring out in the spotlight and goes bing, bing, and the spotlight comes on Jack, and there he is, bald headed, no moustache, and Waring, said, "Out." And that's how come we happened to go down south.
